levels.title: Allah is Our Creator
levels.storyText: A long, long time ago, Allah made the whole world! Allah made the sun, the moon, the stars, the trees, the animals, and YOU. Everything around us — the sky, the flowers, the birds — was made by Allah. Allah loves it when we remember that He made us and everything we see.

questions.question: Who made the sun, the moon, the stars, and YOU?
questions.explanation: Allah is our Creator — He made the whole world and everything in it.

questions.question: What does "Allah is our Creator" mean?
questions.explanation: It means Allah made the whole world and everything in it.

levels.title: Saying Bismillah
levels.storyText: Before we eat or start something good, we say "Bismillah" — "In the name of Allah". Saying Bismillah reminds us that everything we do is with Allah's help. It brings blessings to what we are about to do.

questions.question: What do we say before we eat?
questions.explanation: We say Bismillah — "In the name of Allah" — before we eat or start something good.

questions.question: Why do we say Bismillah?
options: To remember Allah and ask His blessing
questions.explanation: We say Bismillah to remember Allah and ask His blessing on what we do.

levels.title: Saying Alhamdulillah
levels.storyText: When something good happens, or when we finish eating, we say "Alhamdulillah" — "All praise is for Allah". Saying Alhamdulillah shows we are thankful to Allah for all His gifts, like our food, our family, and our health.

questions.question: What do we say to thank Allah?
questions.explanation: We say Alhamdulillah — "All praise is for Allah" — to thank Allah for His gifts.

questions.question: When do we say Alhamdulillah?
options: When we are thankful to Allah
questions.explanation: We say Alhamdulillah when we are thankful to Allah for His gifts.

levels.title: The Shahada
levels.storyText: The Shahada is the first pillar of Islam. It says: "There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger." When we say the Shahada with our heart, we are telling everyone we are Muslim. It is the most important words a Muslim says.

questions.question: What is the Shahada?
options: There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger
questions.explanation: The Shahada says: There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger.

questions.question: Why is the Shahada special?
options: It is the first pillar and shows we are Muslim
questions.explanation: The Shahada is the first pillar of Islam and shows we are Muslim.

levels.title: Salah — Prayer
levels.storyText: Muslims pray to Allah five times every day. This prayer is called Salah. We pray in the morning, at noon, in the afternoon, at sunset, and at night. Salah helps us remember Allah all day long and keeps our heart clean.

questions.question: How many times a day do Muslims pray Salah?
questions.explanation: Muslims pray Salah five times every day.

questions.question: What does Salah help us do?
questions.explanation: Salah helps us remember Allah all day long.

levels.title: Zakat — Sharing
levels.storyText: Zakat is sharing some of our money and things with people who need help. When we have enough, Allah asks us to give a little to the poor. Zakat helps everyone have what they need and keeps our hearts kind.

questions.question: What is Zakat?
options: Sharing with people who need help
questions.explanation: Zakat is sharing some of our money and things with people who need help.

questions.question: Why do we give Zakat?
options: To help the poor and keep our heart kind
questions.explanation: We give Zakat to help the poor and keep our heart kind.

levels.title: Sawm — Fasting
levels.storyText: In the month of Ramadan, Muslims fast from sunrise to sunset. Fasting means we do not eat or drink while the sun is up. It helps us feel what poor people feel and makes us thankful for our food.

questions.question: What does fasting in Ramadan mean?
options: Not eating or drinking while the sun is up
questions.explanation: Fasting means not eating or drinking while the sun is up, in the month of Ramadan.

questions.question: What month do Muslims fast in?
questions.explanation: Muslims fast in the month of Ramadan.

levels.title: Hajj — The Kaaba
levels.storyText: Once a year, Muslims travel to Makkah to visit the Kaaba, the holy house of Allah. This trip is called Hajj. Millions of Muslims go around the Kaaba together and pray. It is a very special journey.

questions.question: Where do Muslims go for Hajj?
questions.explanation: For Hajj, Muslims travel to the Kaaba in Makkah.

questions.question: What is the Kaaba?
questions.explanation: The Kaaba is the holy house of Allah in Makkah.

levels.title: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)
levels.storyText: Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is our teacher and the last prophet of Allah. He taught us to be kind, honest, and good to everyone. We love him and follow his example in everything we do.

questions.question: Who is Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
options: Our teacher and the last prophet of Allah
questions.explanation: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) is our teacher and the last prophet of Allah.

questions.question: What did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) teach us?
options: To be kind, honest, and good
questions.explanation: He taught us to be kind, honest, and good to everyone.

levels.title: The Holy Qur'an
levels.storyText: The Qur'an is Allah's holy book. Allah gave it to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) through Angel Jibril. The Qur'an teaches us how to live a good life and make Allah happy. We read it with love and respect.

questions.question: What is the Qur'an?
questions.explanation: The Qur'an is Allah's holy book, given to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).

questions.question: Who brought the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
questions.explanation: Angel Jibril brought the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).

levels.title: Kindness to Parents
levels.storyText: Allah loves it when we are kind to our parents. We listen to them, speak softly, and help them. Our parents love us and care for us, so we show them love and respect every day.

questions.question: How do we treat our parents?
questions.explanation: We treat our parents with kindness and respect, and help them.

questions.question: Why does Allah love kindness to parents?
options: Because they love and care for us
questions.explanation: Allah loves kindness to parents because they love and care for us.

levels.title: Kindness to Animals
levels.storyText: Allah made the animals, and He wants us to be kind to them. We give water to thirsty animals, feed them, and never hurt them. Even feeding a small bird is a good deed that Allah loves.

questions.question: How should we treat animals?
options: With kindness — feed and give them water
questions.explanation: We should be kind to animals — feed them and give them water, and never hurt them.

questions.question: What is a good deed we can do for animals?
options: Give water to a thirsty animal
questions.explanation: Giving water to a thirsty animal is a good deed Allah loves.

levels.title: Being Honest (Siddiq)
levels.storyText: Being honest means telling the truth, even when it is hard. Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was called Al-Amin — the trustworthy — because he always told the truth. Allah loves honest people.

questions.question: What does being honest mean?
questions.explanation: Being honest means always telling the truth, even when it is hard.

questions.question: What was Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) called for being honest?
questions.explanation: He was called Al-Amin — the trustworthy — because he always told the truth.

levels.title: Smiling is Charity
levels.storyText: Did you know that smiling at someone is a kind of charity? When you smile at your family and friends, you make them happy, and Allah rewards you for it. A smile is a small gift that costs nothing.

questions.question: What is a kind of charity we can give every day?
questions.explanation: Smiling at someone is a kind of charity that Allah rewards.

questions.question: Why is smiling special?
options: It makes people happy and Allah rewards us
questions.explanation: Smiling makes people happy and Allah rewards us for it.

levels.title: Cleanliness is Half of Faith
levels.storyText: Islam teaches us to be clean. We wash our hands, keep our clothes tidy, and do wudu before prayer. Being clean keeps us healthy and makes Allah happy. Cleanliness is half of our faith!

questions.question: What is half of our faith?
questions.explanation: Cleanliness is half of our faith. We keep our body and clothes clean.

questions.question: What do we do before prayer to be clean?
questions.explanation: Before prayer we do wudu — washing — to be clean.

levels.title: Respecting Elders
levels.storyText: Elders are older people like our grandparents and teachers. We respect them by listening, speaking kindly, and helping them. Allah loves it when we show respect to people older than us.

questions.question: How do we respect elders?
options: Listen and speak kindly to them
questions.explanation: We respect elders by listening, speaking kindly, and helping them.

questions.question: Who are our elders?
options: Older people like grandparents and teachers
questions.explanation: Our elders are older people like our grandparents and teachers.

levels.title: Sharing Toys & Food
levels.storyText: Sharing is a beautiful habit. When we share our toys and food with our brothers, sisters, and friends, Allah is happy with us. Sharing makes everyone feel loved and brings more blessings to us.

questions.question: What does Allah love that we share?
questions.explanation: Allah loves it when we share our toys and food with others.

questions.question: Why is sharing good?
options: It makes everyone feel loved and Allah is happy
questions.explanation: Sharing makes everyone feel loved and Allah is happy with us.

levels.title: Saying Assalamu Alaikum
levels.storyText: When Muslims meet, they say "Assalamu Alaikum" — "Peace be upon you". It is a beautiful greeting that spreads peace and love. The reply is "Wa Alaikum Assalam" — "And peace be upon you too".

questions.question: What do Muslims say when they meet?
questions.explanation: Muslims say "Assalamu Alaikum" — "Peace be upon you" — when they meet.

questions.question: What is the reply to Assalamu Alaikum?
questions.explanation: The reply is "Wa Alaikum Assalam" — "And peace be upon you too".

levels.title: Prophet Adam (AS)
levels.storyText: Prophet Adam (peace be upon him) was the first human Allah ever made. Allah made him from clay and gave him knowledge. Allah taught Adam the names of everything. He was the father of all people.

questions.question: Who was the first human Allah made?
questions.explanation: Prophet Adam (AS) was the first human Allah ever made.

questions.question: What did Allah give Prophet Adam (AS)?
options: Knowledge and taught him the names of everything
questions.explanation: Allah gave Adam knowledge and taught him the names of everything.

levels.title: Prophet Nuh (AS)
levels.storyText: Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him) told his people to worship only Allah, but most did not listen. Allah told him to build a great ark — a big boat. Nuh took the believers and pairs of every animal on the ark. A great flood came, and the ark kept them safe.

questions.question: What did Prophet Nuh (AS) build?
options: A great ark — a big boat
questions.explanation: Prophet Nuh (AS) built a great ark that kept the believers and animals safe from the flood.

questions.question: Who did Prophet Nuh (AS) tell people to worship?
questions.explanation: Prophet Nuh (AS) told people to worship only Allah.

levels.title: Prophet Ibrahim (AS)
levels.storyText: Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him) loved Allah so much that he was called the Friend of Allah. He told people to stop worshipping idols and worship only Allah. He was ready to give up everything for Allah, and Allah saved him.

questions.question: Why was Prophet Ibrahim (AS) called the Friend of Allah?
options: Because he loved Allah and worshipped only Him
questions.explanation: Prophet Ibrahim (AS) was called the Friend of Allah because he loved Allah and worshipped only Him.

questions.question: What did Prophet Ibrahim (AS) tell people to stop doing?
questions.explanation: He told people to stop worshipping idols and worship only Allah.

levels.title: Prophet Yunus (AS)
levels.storyText: Prophet Yunus (peace be upon him) left his people without Allah's permission. A huge whale swallowed him! Inside the whale, he prayed to Allah: "There is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong." Allah heard him and the whale let him go.

questions.question: What animal swallowed Prophet Yunus (AS)?
questions.explanation: A huge whale swallowed Prophet Yunus (AS) after he left his people.

questions.question: What did Prophet Yunus (AS) do inside the whale?
options: He prayed to Allah and asked forgiveness
questions.explanation: Inside the whale, Prophet Yunus (AS) prayed to Allah and asked for forgiveness.

levels.title: Prophet Musa (AS)
levels.storyText: Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) led his people away from a cruel king. When they reached the sea, Allah told Musa to strike the water with his staff. The sea parted into two walls, and Musa and his people crossed safely!

questions.question: What miracle did Allah give Prophet Musa (AS) at the sea?
options: The sea parted so his people could cross
questions.explanation: Allah parted the sea so Prophet Musa (AS) and his people could cross safely.

questions.question: What did Musa (AS) use to strike the water?
questions.explanation: Musa (AS) struck the water with his staff, and the sea parted.

levels.title: Prophet Isa (AS)
levels.storyText: Prophet Isa (peace be upon him) was born by a great miracle from Allah. He was kind to the poor and the sick, and Allah gave him the power to heal people. He taught people to worship only Allah.

questions.question: What miracle did Allah give Prophet Isa (AS)?
questions.explanation: Allah gave Prophet Isa (AS) the power to heal the sick.

questions.question: What did Prophet Isa (AS) teach people?
questions.explanation: Prophet Isa (AS) taught people to worship only Allah.

levels.title: Angel Jibril (AS)
levels.storyText: Angel Jibril (peace be upon him) is a special angel who brings Allah's words to the prophets. He brought the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). Angels always obey Allah and never do wrong.

questions.question: Who brings Allah's words to the prophets?
questions.explanation: Angel Jibril (AS) brings Allah's words to the prophets.

questions.question: What did Angel Jibril bring to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
questions.explanation: Angel Jibril brought the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad (PBUH).

levels.title: The Kaaba
levels.storyText: The Kaaba is the holy house of Allah in Makkah. It is a big black cube, and Muslims all over the world face it when they pray. It was first built by Prophet Ibrahim (AS) and his son Ismail (AS).

questions.question: What is the Kaaba?
questions.explanation: The Kaaba is Allah's holy house in Makkah.

questions.question: Who first built the Kaaba?
options: Prophet Ibrahim (AS) and his son Ismail (AS)
questions.explanation: The Kaaba was first built by Prophet Ibrahim (AS) and his son Ismail (AS).

levels.title: Ramadan & Eid
levels.storyText: Ramadan is the month we fast and do extra good deeds. At the end of Ramadan, we celebrate Eid al-Fitr! We pray together, give gifts, wear our best clothes, and share food with family and friends.

questions.question: What do we celebrate at the end of Ramadan?
questions.explanation: At the end of Ramadan we celebrate Eid al-Fitr.

questions.question: What do we do on Eid?
options: Pray, give gifts, and share food with family
questions.explanation: On Eid we pray together, give gifts, wear nice clothes, and share food with family.

levels.title: Making Dua
levels.storyText: Dua is talking to Allah. Any time, any place, we can raise our hands and ask Allah for help, say thank you, or tell Him how we feel. Allah always hears our dua and loves it when we talk to Him.

questions.question: What is dua?
questions.explanation: Dua is talking to Allah — asking for help or saying thank you.

questions.question: When can we make dua?
questions.explanation: We can make dua any time and any place — Allah always hears us.

levels.title: Forgiving Others
levels.storyText: Sometimes people hurt our feelings. Allah loves it when we forgive them instead of being angry. Forgiving means letting go of anger and being kind, just like we hope Allah forgives us.

questions.question: What does Allah love when someone hurts our feelings?
questions.explanation: Allah loves it when we forgive others instead of staying angry.

questions.question: Why do we forgive others?
options: Because we hope Allah forgives us
questions.explanation: We forgive others because we hope Allah will forgive us too.

levels.title: Being a Good Companion
levels.storyText: A good Muslim companion is a good friend. We help our friends do good, speak kindly, and never hurt anyone. The Prophet (PBUH) said a good friend is like a seller of good perfume — being near them makes you better.

questions.question: What is a good Muslim companion like?
options: A good friend who helps us do good
Someone who tells us to lie
questions.explanation: A good Muslim companion is a good friend who helps us do good.

questions.question: What did the Prophet (PBUH) say a good friend is like?
options: A seller of good perfume — being near them makes you better
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said a good friend is like a seller of good perfume — being near them makes you better.

levels.title: The 5 Pillars of Islam
levels.storyText: Islam stands on five pillars: Shahada (the declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (giving charity), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), and Hajj (the pilgrimage to Makkah). These five duties are the foundation of a Muslim's life and worship.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the five pillars?
questions.explanation: The five pillars are Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj — Eid shopping is not one.

questions.question: Name the five pillars of Islam.
questions.explanation: The five pillars are Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj.

levels.title: The 6 Articles of Iman
levels.storyText: Iman (faith) has six articles: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine destiny (Qadar). Believing in all six is what makes a Muslim's faith complete.

questions.question: How many articles of Iman are there?
questions.explanation: There are six articles of Iman (faith).

questions.question: Which is one of the six articles of Iman?
questions.explanation: Belief in Allah's angels is one of the six articles of Iman.

levels.title: Shahada in Detail
levels.storyText: The Shahada has two parts: "There is no god but Allah" — meaning Allah alone deserves worship; and "Muhammad is His messenger" — meaning we follow the Prophet's example. Saying it with belief makes someone a Muslim.

questions.question: What are the two parts of the Shahada?
options: No god but Allah; Muhammad is His messenger
Allah is great; pray five times
questions.explanation: The Shahada is: There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is His messenger.

questions.question: What does "no god but Allah" mean?
questions.explanation: It means Allah alone deserves worship and there is no other god.

levels.title: Salah in Detail
levels.storyText: Salah is the five daily prayers: Fajr (dawn), Dhuhr (noon), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), and Isha (night). Each prayer has its own time, and we pray facing the Kaaba in Makkah.

questions.question: Which is the dawn prayer?
questions.explanation: Fajr is the dawn prayer, prayed before sunrise.

questions.question: List the five daily prayers in order.
questions.explanation: The five daily prayers are Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha.

levels.title: Zakat in Detail
levels.storyText: Zakat is giving a set share (usually 2.5%) of our saved wealth to the poor each year. It purifies our money and helps people in need. Zakat is a duty on every Muslim who has enough savings.

questions.question: What share of saved wealth is Zakat usually?
questions.explanation: Zakat is usually 2.5% of our saved wealth given each year.

questions.question: Who must pay Zakat?
options: A Muslim who has enough saved wealth
questions.explanation: Zakat is a duty on every Muslim who has enough saved wealth.

levels.title: Steps of Wudu
levels.storyText: Wudu is the washing we do before Salah. We wash our hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, wipe our head and ears, and wash our feet — all in order. Wudu must be done with clean water and a sincere intention (niyyah).

questions.question: What do we do before Salah to become clean?
questions.explanation: We do wudu — washing in order — before Salah to become clean.

questions.question: What is the first step of wudu?
options: Wash the hands and make niyyah
questions.explanation: The first step of wudu is to wash the hands and make the intention (niyyah).

levels.title: Niyyah — Intention
levels.storyText: Niyyah is the intention in our heart before any worship. Before wudu, Salah, or fasting, we make a quiet intention that we are doing this only for Allah. Without a sincere niyyah, the action is not accepted.

questions.question: What is niyyah?
options: The intention in our heart for Allah
questions.explanation: Niyyah is the intention in our heart that we are worshipping only for Allah.

questions.question: Why is niyyah important in worship?
options: Without it the action is not accepted
questions.explanation: Without a sincere niyyah, our worship is not accepted by Allah.

levels.title: Salah Positions
levels.storyText: Salah has set positions: standing (Qiyam), bowing (Ruku), prostration (Sujud), and sitting (Tashahhud). Each position has its own words. Sujud is the closest we can be to Allah, so we make extra dua in it.

questions.question: Which position in Salah is closest to Allah?
questions.explanation: Sujud (prostration) is the position in which we are closest to Allah.

questions.question: Name the main positions of Salah.
questions.explanation: The main positions are Qiyam (standing), Ruku (bowing), Sujud (prostration), and Tashahhud (sitting).

levels.title: Sawm in Detail
levels.storyText: Fasting (Sawm) in Ramadan means no food, drink, or bad behaviour from dawn (Fajr) to sunset (Maghrib). We also avoid arguing and lying. Fasting teaches patience (Sabr) and makes us feel what the poor feel.

questions.question: From which prayer to which prayer do we fast?
questions.explanation: We fast from Fajr (dawn) to Maghrib (sunset).

questions.question: What does fasting teach us?
options: Patience and empathy with the poor
questions.explanation: Fasting teaches patience (Sabr) and makes us feel what the poor feel.

levels.title: Hajj in Detail
levels.storyText: Hajj is the pilgrimage to Makkah once in a lifetime for those who can. Pilgrims wear simple white clothes (Ihram), walk around the Kaaba (Tawaf), and run between Safa and Marwa. It reminds us that all people are equal before Allah.

questions.question: What do pilgrims wear for Hajj?
questions.explanation: Pilgrims wear simple white clothes called Ihram for Hajj.

questions.question: What is walking around the Kaaba called?
questions.explanation: Walking around the Kaaba is called Tawaf.

levels.title: Prophet Ibrahim's Sacrifice
levels.storyText: Allah tested Prophet Ibrahim (AS) by asking him to sacrifice his son. Ibrahim (AS) was ready to obey Allah. Allah replaced his son with a ram — a mercy from Allah. This obedience is remembered every Eid al-Adha.

questions.question: What did Allah replace with a ram?
questions.explanation: Allah replaced Ibrahim's sacrifice of his son with a ram as a mercy.

questions.question: Which Eid remembers Ibrahim's obedience?
questions.explanation: Eid al-Adha remembers Prophet Ibrahim's (AS) obedience to Allah.

levels.title: Prophet Yusuf's Patience
levels.storyText: Prophet Yusuf (peace be upon him) was thrown into a well by his jealous brothers, then sold as a slave, then jailed wrongly. Through all of this he kept his patience (Sabr) and his trust in Allah. Allah raised him to a high position in Egypt.

questions.question: What did Prophet Yusuf's (AS) brothers do to him?
questions.explanation: His jealous brothers threw Prophet Yusuf (AS) into a well.

questions.question: What quality did Prophet Yusuf (AS) show?
questions.explanation: Prophet Yusuf (AS) showed patience (Sabr) and trust in Allah through all his trials.

levels.title: Prophet Sulaiman's Gratitude
levels.storyText: Prophet Sulaiman (peace be upon him) was a great king with a mighty kingdom and could understand animals. Even with all his power, he always thanked Allah. He said, "This is by the grace of my Lord" — teaching us to be grateful, not proud.

questions.question: What special gift did Allah give Prophet Sulaiman (AS)?
questions.explanation: Allah gave Prophet Sulaiman (AS) the ability to understand animals.

questions.question: What did Prophet Sulaiman (AS) always say about his blessings?
options: "This is by the grace of my Lord"
questions.explanation: He always said, "This is by the grace of my Lord" — teaching gratitude, not pride.

levels.title: Amanah — Trustworthiness
levels.storyText: Amanah means being trustworthy — keeping promises, returning what is entrusted to you, and never betraying trust. Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was called Al-Amin even before prophethood because everyone trusted him.

questions.question: What does Amanah mean?
questions.explanation: Amanah means being trustworthy, keeping promises, and never betraying trust.

questions.question: Why was Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) called Al-Amin?
questions.explanation: He was called Al-Amin because everyone trusted him to keep his promises.

levels.title: Sabr — Patience
levels.storyText: Sabr is patience — staying calm and trusting Allah when things are hard. Sabr is not just waiting; it is doing the right thing without complaining. Allah is with those who are patient (Sabireen).

questions.question: What is Sabr?
options: Patience and trusting Allah in hard times
questions.explanation: Sabr is patience — staying calm and trusting Allah when things are hard.

questions.question: Who is Allah with, according to the Qur'an?
questions.explanation: Allah is with those who are patient (the Sabireen).

levels.title: Controlling Anger
levels.storyText: The Prophet (PBUH) taught us to control anger. He said the strong person is not the one who wrestles others, but the one who controls himself when angry. A simple tip is to sit down or make wudu when angry.

questions.question: Who is the truly strong person, according to the Prophet (PBUH)?
options: The one who controls himself when angry
The one who can lift the most
questions.explanation: The strong person is the one who controls himself when angry.

questions.question: What did the Prophet (PBUH) advise when angry?
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) advised sitting down or making wudu when angry.

levels.title: Etiquette of Sleeping
levels.storyText: Before sleeping, we brush our teeth, make wudu, dust the bed three times, and sleep on our right side. We recite the bedtime duas and the last verses of Surah Al-Baqarah. This protects us through the night.

questions.question: Which side did the Prophet (PBUH) sleep on?
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) slept on his right side.

questions.question: What should we do before sleeping?
options: Make wudu and recite bedtime duas
questions.explanation: Before sleeping we make wudu, dust the bed, and recite bedtime duas.

levels.title: Etiquette of Eating
levels.storyText: We eat with the right hand, say Bismillah before eating, and Alhamdulillah after. We do not complain about food and we do not waste. The Prophet (PBUH) taught us to eat what is in front of us and share with others.

questions.question: Which hand do we eat with?
questions.explanation: We eat with the right hand, after saying Bismillah.

questions.question: What do we say before and after eating?
questions.explanation: We say Bismillah before eating and Alhamdulillah after.

levels.title: Etiquette of Entering the Home
levels.storyText: When entering the home, we say Assalamu Alaikum, even if no one is there (greeting the angels). We enter with the right foot and recite a dua. This brings peace and blessings to the home.

questions.question: What do we say when entering the home?
questions.explanation: We say Assalamu Alaikum when entering the home, even if no one is there.

questions.question: Which foot do we enter with?
questions.explanation: We enter the home with the right foot and recite a dua.

levels.title: Seeking Knowledge
levels.storyText: Islam loves seeking knowledge. The Prophet (PBUH) said seeking knowledge is a duty on every Muslim. We ask questions, learn from teachers, and act on what we learn. Knowledge that is acted upon is better than worship without understanding.

questions.question: What did the Prophet (PBUH) say about seeking knowledge?
options: It is a duty on every Muslim
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said seeking knowledge is a duty on every Muslim.

questions.question: Which is better, according to the Prophet (PBUH)?
questions.explanation: Knowledge that is acted upon is better than worship without understanding.

levels.title: Birth of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)
levels.storyText: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was born in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant. His father Abdullah died before he was born, and his mother Aminah raised him with love. He was known for being honest and kind from a young age.

questions.question: Where was Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) born?
questions.explanation: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) was born in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant.

questions.question: What was his father's name?
questions.explanation: His father was Abdullah, who died before the Prophet (PBUH) was born.

levels.title: Cave Hira — First Revelation
levels.storyText: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) used to meditate in the Cave of Hira near Makkah. One night, Angel Jibril came and said "Read!" (Iqra). The first verses of the Qur'an were revealed to him there. This began his prophethood.

questions.question: Where did the Prophet (PBUH) receive the first revelation?
options: On a mountain top in Yemen
questions.explanation: The first revelation came to the Prophet (PBUH) in the Cave of Hira near Makkah.

questions.question: What did Angel Jibril say first?
questions.explanation: Angel Jibril said "Read!" (Iqra) — the first word of the revealed Qur'an.

levels.title: Migration to Madinah
levels.storyText: When the people of Makkah hurt the Muslims, the Prophet (PBUH) and his followers migrated to Madinah. This journey is called the Hijrah, and the Islamic calendar begins from this event. In Madinah, the Muslims built the first mosque and lived in peace.

questions.question: What is the migration to Madinah called?
questions.explanation: The migration to Madinah is called the Hijrah.

questions.question: What does the Islamic calendar begin from?
questions.explanation: The Islamic (Hijri) calendar begins from the Hijrah — the migration to Madinah.

levels.title: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
levels.storyText: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was a peace agreement between the Muslims of Madinah and the people of Makkah. Even though some terms seemed unfair, the Prophet (PBUH) agreed to it for peace. It brought years of calm and allowed Islam to spread.

questions.question: What was the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah?
options: A peace agreement between Madinah and Makkah
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was a peace agreement between the Muslims and the people of Makkah.

questions.question: Why did the Prophet (PBUH) agree to the treaty?
options: To bring peace and let Islam spread
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) agreed to the treaty to bring peace and allow Islam to spread.

levels.title: Sadaqah — Charity
levels.storyText: Sadaqah is any voluntary charity — money, food, a smile, or help. Unlike Zakat, Sadaqah has no fixed amount and can be given any time. The Prophet (PBUH) said even a kind word is Sadaqah. It protects us from harm and increases our blessings.

questions.question: What is Sadaqah?
questions.explanation: Sadaqah is voluntary charity of any kind — money, food, or even a kind word.

questions.question: How is Sadaqah different from Zakat?
options: Sadaqah is voluntary with no fixed amount; Zakat is a fixed duty
Sadaqah is only for the rich
questions.explanation: Sadaqah is voluntary with no fixed amount, while Zakat is a fixed duty on saved wealth.

levels.title: Respecting the Qur'an
levels.storyText: The Qur'an is Allah's word, so we treat it with deep respect. We keep it clean, place it on a high shelf, and do not put other things on top of it. We recite it with care and try to understand what it means.

questions.question: How should we treat the Qur'an?
options: With deep respect and keep it clean
Under our pillow with junk on top
questions.explanation: We treat the Qur'an with deep respect — keeping it clean and on a high place.

questions.question: Can we put other books on top of the Qur'an?
options: No, we keep it on top or in a high clean place
questions.explanation: No — we keep the Qur'an on top or in a high, clean place, not under other things.

levels.title: The Five Daily Prayers — Times
levels.storyText: Each prayer has a window of time: Fajr (before sunrise), Dhuhr (just after noon), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (just after sunset), and Isha (night). Praying on time is one of the most beloved deeds to Allah.

questions.question: When is Dhuhr prayed?
questions.explanation: Dhuhr is prayed just after noon.

questions.question: When is Maghrib prayed?
questions.explanation: Maghrib is prayed just after sunset.

levels.title: Dua after Salah
levels.storyText: After the prayer, we can make dua — raising our hands and asking Allah. This is a special time when duas are accepted. We can ask for forgiveness, blessings for our family, and guidance.

questions.question: What can we do right after Salah?
questions.explanation: After Salah we can make dua — it is a special time when duas are accepted.

questions.question: Why is dua after Salah special?
options: It is a time when duas are accepted
It is when everyone is busy
questions.explanation: Right after Salah is a special time when duas are accepted by Allah.

levels.title: Review of Seerah
levels.storyText: The Seerah is the story of the Prophet's (PBUH) life — his birth, his honesty in Makkah, his prophethood at the Cave of Hira, his patience through hardship, the Hijrah to Madinah, and the years of peace. Studying the Seerah helps us love and follow him.

questions.question: What is the Seerah?
options: The story of the Prophet's (PBUH) life
questions.explanation: The Seerah is the story of Prophet Muhammad's (PBUH) life.

questions.question: Why do we study the Seerah?
options: To love and follow the Prophet (PBUH)
questions.explanation: We study the Seerah to love and follow the Prophet (PBUH) in our lives.

levels.title: Being a Role Model
levels.storyText: A good Muslim is a role model — honest, kind, and helpful. The Prophet (PBUH) was the best role model. By following his character, we become people others look up to and trust, and we please Allah.

questions.question: Who is the best role model for Muslims?
questions.explanation: Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) is the best role model for Muslims.

questions.question: How do we become a good role model?
options: By being honest, kind, and helpful
questions.explanation: We become a good role model by being honest, kind, and helpful — following the Prophet's (PBUH) character.

levels.title: Tafsir of Surah Al-Fatiha
levels.storyText: Surah Al-Fatiha, "The Opening", is the mother of the Qur'an and is recited in every unit of Salah. It praises Allah as the Lord of all worlds, the Most Merciful, the Master of the Day of Judgement. We worship only Him and ask Him to guide us on the straight path — not the path of those who earned His anger or went astray.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the meaning of Surah Al-Fatiha.
options: It is the Opening — we praise Allah as Lord of all worlds and ask Him to guide us on the straight path
It is about Allah being one with no partner
It is about seeking refuge from evil
It is about the morning light
questions.explanation: Surah Al-Fatiha is the Opening — it praises Allah as Lord of all worlds, the Most Merciful, the Master of the Day of Judgement, and asks Him to guide us on the straight path.

questions.question: Which verse of Al-Fatiha asks for guidance?
options: Guide us on the straight path
questions.explanation: The verse "Guide us on the straight path" asks Allah for guidance.

levels.title: Tafsir of Surah Al-Ikhlas
levels.storyText: Surah Al-Ikhlas, "Sincerity", declares the absolute oneness of Allah. It says Allah is One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, and there is none comparable to Him. It is a powerful statement of Tawheed — that Allah is unique, absolute, and unlike any creation.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the meaning of Surah Al-Ikhlas.
options: It declares Allah is One, the Eternal Refuge, who does not beget nor is He begotten, and none is comparable to Him
It is the Opening asking for guidance on the straight path
It is about seeking refuge from the evil whisperer
It is about the morning light and silence
questions.explanation: Surah Al-Ikhlas declares the absolute oneness of Allah — He is One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is begotten, and none is comparable to Him.

questions.question: Which concept does Surah Al-Ikhlas teach?
options: Tawheed — the absolute oneness and uniqueness of Allah
questions.explanation: Surah Al-Ikhlas teaches Tawheed — the absolute oneness and uniqueness of Allah.

levels.title: Tafsir of Surah Al-Falaq
levels.storyText: Surah Al-Falaq, "The Daybreak", is a prayer for refuge. We seek Allah's protection from the evil of what He created, from the darkness of night, from those who practise witchcraft, and from the envier when he envies. It teaches us to turn to Allah for safety from all harms.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the meaning of Surah Al-Falaq.
options: It is a prayer seeking Allah's refuge from the evil of creation, the night, witchcraft, and envy
It declares Allah is One and absolute
It praises Allah as Lord of all worlds
It is about the morning light of guidance
questions.explanation: Surah Al-Falaq is a prayer seeking Allah's refuge from the evil of what He created, the darkness of night, witchcraft, and the envier.

questions.question: From what does Surah Al-Falaq seek refuge?
options: The evil of creation, night, witchcraft, and envy
questions.explanation: It seeks refuge from the evil of creation, the darkness of night, witchcraft, and the envier.

levels.title: Tafsir of Surah An-Nas
levels.storyText: Surah An-Nas, "Mankind", seeks refuge in Allah from the evil of the whisperer (waswas) who whispers into the hearts of people — both from among the jinn and mankind. It teaches us to guard our heart from doubts and bad thoughts by turning to Allah.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the meaning of Surah An-Nas.
options: It seeks refuge in Allah from the whisperer who whispers into the hearts of people, from jinn and mankind
It declares Allah is One who does not beget
It seeks refuge from the evil of creation and envy
It praises Allah as Lord of all worlds
questions.explanation: Surah An-Nas seeks refuge in Allah from the whisperer (waswas) who whispers into the hearts of people — from jinn and mankind.

questions.question: From whom does Surah An-Nas seek refuge?
options: The whisperer who whispers into hearts, from jinn and mankind
questions.explanation: It seeks refuge from the whisperer (waswas) who whispers into the hearts of people — from jinn and mankind.

levels.title: Connecting the Four Quls
levels.storyText: The four short surahs often called the "Quls" — Al-Kafirun, Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, and An-Nas — are recited for protection and to strengthen faith. Al-Kafirun rejects false worship, Al-Ikhlas affirms Tawheed, and Al-Falaq and An-Nas seek refuge from outer and inner harms.

questions.question: Which surah affirms the absolute oneness of Allah among the four Quls?
questions.explanation: Al-Ikhlas affirms the absolute oneness (Tawheed) of Allah among the four Quls.

questions.question: Which two surahs among the Quls seek refuge from harm?
questions.explanation: Al-Falaq and An-Nas seek refuge from outer and inner harms.

levels.title: Hadith 1 — Intention
levels.storyText: The first hadith of the Forty Hadith of Imam Nawawi states: "Actions are but by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended." This teaches that the value of any deed depends on the sincere intention behind it — done for Allah alone.

questions.question: What does the first hadith of Imam Nawawi teach?
options: Actions are judged by their intention
We should eat with the right hand
questions.explanation: It teaches that actions are judged by intentions — every person gets only what they intended.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the meaning of this hadith.
options: The value of a deed depends on the sincere intention behind it, done for Allah alone
The number of deeds matters more than the heart
questions.explanation: A deed's value depends on the sincere intention (niyyah) behind it — done for Allah alone.

levels.title: Hadith 2 — Islam, Iman, Ihsan
levels.storyText: The second hadith (the Hadith of Jibril) defines the religion: Islam is the five pillars, Iman is belief in Allah, angels, books, messengers, the Last Day, and Qadar; and Ihsan is to worship Allah as if you see Him, for even if you do not see Him, He sees you.

questions.question: What does Ihsan mean in the Hadith of Jibril?
options: To worship Allah as if you see Him, and if not, know He sees you
questions.explanation: Ihsan is to worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not, to know that He sees you.

questions.question: List the three parts of the religion in the Hadith of Jibril.
questions.explanation: The religion has three parts: Islam, Iman, and Ihsan.

levels.title: Hadith 3 — Pillars of Islam
levels.storyText: The third hadith states that Islam is built on five pillars: testifying that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His messenger, establishing Salah, giving Zakat, fasting Ramadan, and performing Hajj for those who are able.

questions.question: What are the five pillars mentioned in this hadith?
questions.explanation: The five pillars are the Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj.

questions.question: In your own words, what does this hadith teach?
options: Islam is built on five pillars — the Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj
questions.explanation: Islam is built on five pillars: Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj.

levels.title: Hadith 4 — Stages of Creation
levels.storyText: The fourth hadith explains that each person is created in stages: a drop, then a clot, then a lump, then bones clothed with flesh. The soul is breathed in, and life is decreed. It teaches us about Allah's power over our existence.

questions.question: What does the fourth hadith describe?
options: The stages of human creation in the womb
questions.explanation: It describes the stages of human creation in the womb.

questions.question: What is breathed into the body during creation?
questions.explanation: The soul (ruh) is breathed into the body during creation.

levels.title: Hadith 5 — Rejecting Innovation
levels.storyText: The fifth hadith warns: "Whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that does not belong to it, it is rejected." This teaches us to follow the religion as the Prophet (PBUH) taught it, and to avoid innovated practices (bid'ah) that have no basis in Islam.

questions.question: What does the fifth hadith teach about innovation?
options: Innovations not part of the religion are rejected
questions.explanation: It teaches that any innovation not belonging to the religion is rejected.

questions.question: In your own words, explain this hadith.
options: We must follow the religion as the Prophet (PBUH) taught it, and avoid innovated practices with no basis
We must change the pillars every year
We must follow whatever is popular
questions.explanation: We follow the religion as the Prophet (PBUH) taught it, and avoid innovated practices (bid'ah) with no basis in Islam.

levels.title: Ibn Sina — Medicine
levels.storyText: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) was a great Muslim scholar of the Golden Age. He wrote "The Canon of Medicine", which was used in European universities for centuries. He saw the pursuit of knowledge as an act of worship, since understanding Allah's creation deepens faith.

questions.question: What famous book did Ibn Sina write?
questions.explanation: Ibn Sina wrote "The Canon of Medicine", used in European universities for centuries.

questions.question: How did Ibn Sina see the pursuit of knowledge?
options: As an act of worship that deepens faith
As a way to get rich
questions.explanation: He saw the pursuit of knowledge as an act of worship that deepens faith.

levels.title: Al-Khwarizmi — Algebra
levels.storyText: Al-Khwarizmi was a Muslim mathematician whose work gave us the word "algebra". He introduced systematic ways to solve equations and brought Arabic numerals to the world. His work laid the foundation for modern mathematics and computing.

questions.question: What field did Al-Khwarizmi help found?
questions.explanation: Al-Khwarizmi's work gave us the word "algebra" and laid the foundation for modern mathematics.

questions.question: What numerals did Al-Khwarizmi help spread?
questions.explanation: Al-Khwarizmi helped spread Arabic numerals to the world.

levels.title: Fatima al-Fihri — Education
levels.storyText: Fatima al-Fihri was a Muslim woman who founded the Qarawiyyin Mosque and university in Fes, Morocco — the world's oldest continuously running university. She used her inheritance to build a centre of learning that taught for over a thousand years.

questions.question: What did Fatima al-Fihri found?
questions.explanation: Fatima al-Fihri founded the Qarawiyyin Mosque and university in Fes — the world's oldest continuously running university.

questions.question: What did she use to build this centre of learning?
questions.explanation: She used her inheritance to build the Qarawiyyin, a centre of learning that has taught for over a thousand years.

levels.title: The House of Wisdom
levels.storyText: The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikmah) in Baghdad was a great library and translation centre of the Islamic Golden Age. Scholars of many faiths worked together to translate Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic, sparking advances in science, medicine, and philosophy.

questions.question: What was the House of Wisdom?
options: A library and translation centre in Baghdad
questions.explanation: The House of Wisdom was a great library and translation centre in Baghdad during the Golden Age.

questions.question: Who worked at the House of Wisdom?
options: Scholars of many faiths working together
questions.explanation: Scholars of many faiths worked together there, translating works and advancing knowledge.

levels.title: Islamic Golden Age — Values
levels.storyText: The Islamic Golden Age was driven by values the Qur'an and Sunnah encouraged: curiosity, humility, and service. Seeking knowledge was seen as worship; helping the sick and poor was a duty. These values produced advances still shaping the world today.

questions.question: Which value drove the Islamic Golden Age?
options: Curiosity and seeking knowledge as worship
questions.explanation: Curiosity and seeing the seeking of knowledge as worship drove the Golden Age.

questions.question: In your own words, how did Islam encourage science?
options: By teaching that seeking knowledge is worship and serving creation is a duty
questions.explanation: Islam encouraged science by teaching that seeking knowledge is worship and serving creation is a duty.

levels.title: Gheebah — Backbiting
levels.storyText: Gheebah (backbiting) is mentioning something about your brother or sister that they would dislike, even if it is true. The Qur'an compares it to eating the flesh of a dead brother — a powerful image of how harmful it is. We must guard our tongue and speak only good.

questions.question: What is Gheebah?
options: Mentioning something about someone that they would dislike, behind their back
questions.explanation: Gheebah is backbiting — mentioning something about someone that they would dislike, behind their back.

questions.question: What does the Qur'an compare Gheebah to?
options: Eating the flesh of a dead brother
questions.explanation: The Qur'an compares Gheebah to eating the flesh of a dead brother — a powerful image of its harm.

levels.title: Digital Ethics in Islam
levels.storyText: Islamic manners apply online too. We must be truthful, avoid gossip and backbiting, protect privacy, and not spread harmful content. The Prophet (PBUH) taught that a person's tongue can lead them to good or ruin — and that applies to what we type and share.

questions.question: How should a Muslim behave online?
questions.explanation: A Muslim online should be truthful, avoid gossip and backbiting, protect privacy, and not spread harm.

questions.question: In your own words, how does the Sunnah apply to digital life?
options: We guard our tongue and what we type, speaking only good and avoiding harm
We should post often to be famous
questions.explanation: The Sunnah of guarding the tongue applies to what we type and share — speak only good and avoid harm.

levels.title: Mental Wellbeing in the Qur'an
levels.storyText: The Qur'an offers comfort for the heart: "With hardship comes ease" and "Do not despair of Allah's mercy." It teaches us to turn to Allah in sadness, to have sabr (patience), and to seek help through patience and prayer. Mental wellbeing is part of trusting Allah's care.

questions.question: What does the Qur'an say about hardship?
questions.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that with hardship comes ease.

questions.question: How does the Qur'an comfort a sad heart?
options: "Do not despair of Allah's mercy" and seek help through patience and prayer
By telling us to give up
By telling us to be angry
questions.explanation: The Qur'an says "Do not despair of Allah's mercy" and to seek help through patience (sabr) and prayer.

levels.title: Avoiding Gossip Online
levels.storyText: Sharing unverified news or rumours online can harm innocent people and spread fear. Islam teaches us to verify before sharing and to stay silent if in doubt. The Prophet (PBUH) said it is enough for a person to be considered a liar that they repeat everything they hear.

questions.question: What should we do before sharing news online?
options: Verify it first, and stay silent if in doubt
Share it instantly to be first
Share it even if it might be false
Share it if it is exciting
questions.explanation: We must verify news before sharing and stay silent if in doubt, to avoid harm.

questions.question: What did the Prophet (PBUH) say about repeating everything we hear?
options: It is enough for a person to be considered a liar
It is a sign of wisdom
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said it is enough for a person to be considered a liar that they repeat everything they hear.

levels.title: Battle of Badr
levels.storyText: The Battle of Badr was the first major battle in Islamic history. A small Muslim army of about 313 faced a much larger Makkan army. With faith and trust in Allah, the Muslims won. It showed that victory comes from Allah, not just numbers or weapons.

questions.question: Why was the Battle of Badr significant?
options: It was the first major battle, won by a small Muslim army with Allah's help
It ended the Islamic Golden Age
questions.explanation: Badr was the first major battle — a small Muslim army won against a much larger one through Allah's help.

questions.question: In your own words, what does Badr teach?
options: Victory comes from Allah, not just numbers or weapons
questions.explanation: Badr teaches that victory comes from Allah, not from numbers or weapons alone.

levels.title: Battle of Uhud
levels.storyText: The Battle of Uhud was a hard lesson for the early Muslims. The Prophet (PBUH) placed archers on a hill and told them not to leave their posts. When some left to chase the spoils, the enemy attacked from behind. Many Muslims were martyred, including the Prophet's uncle Hamza.

questions.question: What mistake caused the Muslim loss at Uhud?
options: The archers left their posts against the Prophet's orders
questions.explanation: The archers left their hill posts against the Prophet's (PBUH) orders, and the enemy attacked from behind.

questions.question: Who was martyred at Uhud and known as the "Lion of Allah"?
questions.explanation: Hamza, the Prophet's (PBUH) uncle, was martyred at Uhud and is called the "Lion of Allah".

levels.title: Conquest of Makkah
levels.storyText: After years of exile and conflict, the Prophet (PBUH) returned to Makkah with a large army. The Makkans expected revenge, but he forgave them, asking, "What do you think I will do with you?" They said, "A good brother." He replied, "Go, you are free." This was mercy in action.

questions.question: How did the Prophet (PBUH) treat the Makkans when he conquered Makkah?
options: He forgave them and set them free
questions.explanation: He forgave the Makkans, telling them "Go, you are free" — mercy in action.

questions.question: In your own words, what does the Conquest of Makkah teach?
options: That true strength is shown through mercy and forgiveness
questions.explanation: It teaches that true strength is shown through mercy and forgiveness, not revenge.

levels.title: The Farewell Sermon
levels.storyText: In his Farewell Sermon, the Prophet (PBUH) summarised the religion: sanctity of life and property, kindness to women, the end of blood feuds, equality of all races — no Arab over a non-Arab except by piety. He left us the Qur'an and his Sunnah, and asked us to hold firmly to them.

questions.question: What did the Prophet (PBUH) leave us to hold onto?
questions.explanation: He left us the Qur'an and his Sunnah, and asked us to hold firmly to them.

questions.question: What did the Farewell Sermon say about equality?
options: No Arab has superiority over a non-Arab except by piety
questions.explanation: It declared that no Arab has superiority over a non-Arab except by piety.

levels.title: Tawheed — Oneness of Allah
levels.storyText: Tawheed is the core of Islam: Allah is One in His lordship, His worship, and His names and attributes. He has no partner, no equal, and no offspring. Every belief and action in Islam flows from this single truth.

questions.question: What is Tawheed?
options: The oneness of Allah in lordship, worship, and names
questions.explanation: Tawheed is the oneness of Allah — in His lordship, His worship, and His names and attributes.

questions.question: Name the three categories of Tawheed.
questions.explanation: The three categories are Tawheed of Lordship, of Worship, and of Names and Attributes.

levels.title: Purpose of Life
levels.storyText: The Qur'an states our purpose clearly: "I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me." Worship in Islam is not only prayer — it is every good action done sincerely for Allah. Work, study, kindness, and care for family all become worship with the right intention.

questions.question: What does the Qur'an say is the purpose of life?
questions.explanation: The Qur'an says we were created to worship Allah.

questions.question: In your own words, is worship only prayer?
options: No — any good action done sincerely for Allah is worship
questions.explanation: Worship is not only prayer — any good action done sincerely for Allah becomes worship.

levels.title: Mercy in Islam
levels.storyText: Mercy (Rahmah) is at the heart of Islam. Allah's most repeated names are Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem — the Most Merciful. The Prophet (PBUH) was sent as "a mercy to all the worlds". We are taught to be merciful to people, animals, and the earth itself.

questions.question: Which two names of Allah mean "the Most Merciful"?
questions.explanation: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem are the two names of Allah that mean "the Most Merciful".

questions.question: In your own words, what does "mercy to all the worlds" mean?
options: The Prophet (PBUH) was sent as a mercy to all of creation — people, animals, and the earth
It means he was sent only to one city
It means he was sent only for the rich
It means he was sent only for men
questions.explanation: It means the Prophet (PBUH) was sent as a mercy to all of creation — people, animals, and the earth.

levels.title: Leadership in Islam
levels.storyText: Leadership in Islam is a trust (Amanah), not a privilege. The Prophet (PBUH) said a leader of a people is their servant. A Muslim leader is just, consults others (Shura), and puts the welfare of the people before personal gain.

questions.question: How does Islam view leadership?
options: As a trust and a service to the people
As a way to get rich
As a right to be proud
questions.explanation: Islam views leadership as a trust (Amanah) and a service to the people.

questions.question: What did the Prophet (PBUH) say a leader is?
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) said a leader of a people is their servant.

levels.title: Responsibility to Society
levels.storyText: A Muslim is responsible not only for themselves but for their society. We enjoin good and forbid wrong, care for the poor and orphans, and work for justice. The Prophet (PBUH) said all people are like a body — when one part hurts, the whole body suffers.

questions.question: What did the Prophet (PBUH) compare the community to?
options: One body — when one part hurts, all of it suffers
questions.explanation: The Prophet (PBUH) compared the community to one body — when one part hurts, the whole body feels it.

questions.question: In your own words, what is a Muslim's duty to society?
options: To enjoin good, forbid wrong, care for the poor, and work for justice
To mind only one's own business
questions.explanation: A Muslim's duty is to enjoin good, forbid wrong, care for the poor and orphans, and work for justice.

levels.title: Comprehensive Worldview
levels.storyText: A Muslim's worldview is built on Tawheed, purpose, mercy, and responsibility. Every part of life — worship, family, work, society, and the environment — is connected to Allah. This integrated view gives a Muslim balance, meaning, and direction in everything they do.

questions.question: What is at the centre of a Muslim's worldview?
questions.explanation: Tawheed — the oneness of Allah — is at the centre of a Muslim's worldview.

questions.question: In your own words, how does Islam connect all parts of life?
options: Every part of life — worship, family, work, society — is connected to Allah
questions.explanation: Every part of life — worship, family, work, society, and the environment — is connected to Allah.
